q: A male fetus with complete 5α-reductase type 2 deficiency will most likely show which pattern?
o: Normal wolffian derivatives (epididymis, vas, seminal vesicles) but an underdeveloped prostate
Absent seminal vesicles but normal prostate
e: Wolffian structures are driven by fetal testosterone itself, whereas the prostate (from the urogenital sinus) depends mainly on DHT (dihydrotestosterone). Type 2 is the dominant prostatic isoform.
s: Ch 143 Prostate development and physiology

q: For androgen-driven prostate development to occur, a functional androgen receptor is essential in the:
e: Mesenchyme–epithelium signalling drives prostate development. With enough androgen at the right time, even a female urogenital sinus will form prostate.
s: Ch 143 Prostate development and physiology

q: Which statement about androgen metabolism is correct?
o: DHT can be converted back to testosterone
Most plasma testosterone comes from adrenal DHEA
Conversion of testosterone to DHT (5α-reductase) or to oestrogen (aromatase) is irreversible
Testosterone is made in Sertoli cells
e: Testosterone is made in Leydig cells from pregnenolone. Less than 1% of plasma testosterone derives from DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone), and adrenal androgens have only a minor effect on prostate growth.
s: Ch 143 Prostate development and physiology

q: After bilateral orchidectomy, a man becomes functionally castrate within about:
e: Testosterone's plasma half-life is only 10–20 minutes. This is why orchidectomy is the fastest route to castration, for example in spinal cord compression.
s: Ch 143 Prostate development and physiology

q: How does CAG repeat length in the androgen receptor gene affect receptor activity?
e: The shorter the poly-CAG tract, the more active the receptor is in switching on target genes.
s: Ch 143 Prostate development and physiology

q: Which pairing of seminal component and source is correct?
o: Fructose, prostaglandins and semenogelin: seminal vesicle; citrate, zinc, spermine: prostate
e: The seminal vesicles contribute most of the ejaculate volume. Absent fructose in the ejaculate suggests absent seminal vesicles or ejaculatory duct obstruction.
s: Ch 143 Prostate development and physiology

q: Prostate-specific antigen causes liquefaction of semen because it is a:
e: Semenogelin forms the coagulum. Complexed PSA is irreversibly bound to α1-antichymotrypsin and α2-macroglobulin.
s: Ch 143 Prostate development and physiology

q: Which antibiotic group reaches good concentrations in prostatic secretions?
e: Prostatic fluid is more acidic than serum. The drugs that penetrate well include fluoroquinolones, trimethoprim, sulfonamides, tetracyclines, macrolides (erythromycin) and clindamycin.
s: Ch 143 Prostate development and physiology

q: Which α1-adrenoceptor subtype mediates prostatic smooth muscle contraction?
e: α1A predominates in prostatic stroma. α1B is vascular (hence postural hypotension), and α1D is found in bladder and spinal cord.
s: Ch 143 Prostate development and physiology

q: The histological hallmark of BPH is:
o: An increase in the number of epithelial and stromal cells (hyperplasia)
e: Early periurethral nodules are stromal, whereas transition-zone proliferation is glandular. Stroma makes up about 40% of the gland, with prominent smooth muscle.
s: Ch 144 BPH: etiology and natural history

q: Which statement about androgens in BPH is correct?
o: Androgen receptor levels fall with age
Androgens are permissive, not the sole cause, and DHT is about 10 times more potent than testosterone
e: Androgen receptor and DHT levels stay high in the ageing prostate. Androgen withdrawal causes apoptosis.
s: Ch 144 BPH: etiology and natural history

q: Familial BPH is best described as:
o: Autosomal dominant, with larger glands, especially in men needing surgery before 60
e: About 50% of BPH in men having surgery before 60 is estimated to be inheritable.
s: Ch 144 BPH: etiology and natural history

q: Histological (autopsy) BPH:
o: Is found in 100% of men at 40
Is common in men in their twenties
Is uncommon before 30, then rises almost linearly to about 90% of men in their 80s
e: Autopsy studies agree strongly across continents.
s: Ch 144 BPH: etiology and natural history

q: Using the AUA Symptom Index/IPSS, a score of 18 is:
e: Mild 0–7, moderate 8–19, severe 20–35. A change of about 3 points is noticeable to the patient. The IPSS is self-administered and does not ask about incontinence.
s: Ch 144 BPH: etiology and natural history

q: Which statement on prostate volume measurement is correct?
o: MRI usually gives a larger volume than TRUS (transrectal ultrasound)
Transition-zone volume does not change with age
e: TRUS is reliable and reproducible, whereas DRE (digital rectal examination) is poorly reproducible. Volume correlates usefully with serum PSA but not with the degree of obstruction.
s: Ch 144 BPH: etiology and natural history

q: Which factor is associated with a LOWER risk of BPH surgery or prevalence?
o: Heavy alcohol intake and liver cirrhosis
e: Alcohol lowers testosterone, and most autopsy studies show less BPH in cirrhosis (possibly a bias against surgery). Vasectomy has no relation to BPH.
s: Ch 144 BPH: etiology and natural history

q: In the Olmsted County study, which daily medicine was associated with both a higher symptom score and a lower flow rate?
e: Antidepressants, antihistamines and bronchodilators raised scores by 2–3 points, but only antidepressants lowered flow. α-Sympathomimetic cold remedies also worsen LUTS (lower urinary tract symptoms).
s: Ch 144 BPH: etiology and natural history

q: In population-based studies, the strongest predictor of acute urinary retention is:
e: In placebo arms of drug trials (already-diagnosed BPH), PSA and prostate volume are the strongest predictors instead. The difference reflects who was enrolled.
s: Ch 144 BPH: etiology and natural history

q: After spontaneous acute urinary retention, roughly what proportion go on to surgery?
e: After spontaneous retention, 15% have another episode and three-quarters have surgery. After precipitated retention, 9% recur and 26% have surgery.
s: Ch 144 BPH: etiology and natural history

q: Why is acute urinary retention a better end point than surgery in BPH studies?
o: It is a hard, objective event, whereas surgery rates depend on doctor and patient choices and vary by region
e: Most men with BPH never need surgery. Longitudinal population-based cohorts carry the least bias for studying natural history.
s: Ch 144 BPH: etiology and natural history

q: A man with LUTS has a mildly raised creatinine. The most appropriate next test is:
e: Image the upper tracts when creatinine is raised. A smoker with mainly storage symptoms should also have urine cytology to exclude urothelial cancer.
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy

q: A frequency–volume chart for LUTS should ideally cover:
e: Three days balances accuracy against how well patients keep it up. It is especially useful for nocturia and polyuria.
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy

q: PSA testing in a man with LUTS is most appropriate when:
o: He has a life expectancy over 10 years and a cancer diagnosis would change management
e: For example, a 55-year-old with a normal DRE who has never had a PSA test.
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy

q: The gold standard for diagnosing bladder outlet obstruction is:
e: Detrusor overactivity is found in up to 83% of men with severe obstruction, and does not always resolve after treatment.
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy

q: A 50-year-old with IPSS 7 and no risk factors for progression should be offered:
o: Watchful waiting: education, lifestyle and fluid advice, medicine review, and yearly follow-up
e: Lifestyle advice includes sensible fluid intake and cutting down caffeine, tea and alcohol.
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy

q: Which α-blocker needs dose titration when first prescribed?
e: Non-uroselective agents (terazosin, immediate-release doxazosin) carry a high risk of first-dose hypotension. Still warn every patient on any α-blocker.
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy

q: The dizziness and asthenia seen with α1-blockers are thought to be mainly due to:
o: Effects on the central nervous system
e: Postural hypotension is a separate, vascular α1B effect (relative risk about 2.7 for doxazosin vs placebo).
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy

q: Naftopidil is distinctive because it is selective for which receptor?
e: Silodosin is the most α1A-selective. It gave the largest BOOI (bladder outlet obstruction index) reduction (about −30) and has the most ejaculatory dysfunction.
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy

q: Symptom relief with tamsulosin is expected after about:
e: Flow improves within hours. Tamsulosin 0.4 mg and silodosin 8 mg give similar symptom relief.
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy

q: A man taking tamsulosin is listed for cataract surgery. Best advice:
o: Tell the ophthalmologist he takes an α-blocker
e: Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome cannot be reliably prevented by stopping the drug. The surgeon needs to know so they can adapt their technique.
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy

q: Over 6–24 months, 5-ARIs shrink the prostate by about:
e: PSA falls by about 50% (so double the measured value). They reduce the risk of retention and surgery, mainly in larger glands.
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy

q: Which statement about finasteride is correct?
o: It shrinks the prostate within 1 month
It inhibits type 2 5α-reductase and lowers serum DHT by about 70%; volume and flow changes take months
It is a type 1 inhibitor that does not lower serum DHT
e: Correction: the review's answer key calls finasteride a type 1 inhibitor that does not lower DHT. That is wrong. Finasteride inhibits type 2 and lowers serum DHT by about 70%. Dutasteride inhibits types 1 and 2 and lowers it by more than 90%.
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy (book answer corrected)

q: Which adverse effect should patients starting a 5-ARI be warned about, according to the chapter?
e: Large trials found more depressive symptoms. Sexual side effects (libido, erection, ejaculation) and gynaecomastia are the classic ones.
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy

q: In MTOPS, which arm best reduced clinical progression?
e: Doxazosin alone reduced progression compared with placebo but did not reduce invasive therapy. Combination therapy beat both monotherapies.
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy

q: In CombAT, dutasteride monotherapy was better than tamsulosin at:
e: Combination therapy suits large prostates with bothersome voiding symptoms.
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy

q: An antimuscarinic for a man with BPH and storage symptoms should be avoided when:
e: Trials enrolled only men with a residual below 200 mL. Mirabegron is better tolerated in older men with mainly storage symptoms.
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy

q: Daily PDE5 inhibitor monotherapy for LUTS:
o: Lowers IPSS by about 2–4 points more than placebo, without a significant flow improvement
e: It relaxes smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck through nitric oxide and cGMP.
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy

q: Meta-analysis of Serenoa repens (saw palmetto) vs placebo showed:
o: No difference in symptoms or flow
e: Its mechanism is unknown, and extracts differ between products. Some data support the hexane extract.
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy

q: After a first episode of acute urinary retention, a trial without catheter succeeds in about:
e: Start an α-blocker before the trial without catheter to improve the chance of success. Recurrent retention is an indication for surgery.
s: Ch 145 BPH evaluation and medical therapy

q: During monopolar TURP under spinal anaesthesia the patient becomes confused, hypertensive and bradycardic, with sodium 110 mmol/L. Best management:
o: Lower the irrigation, control bleeding, stop the operation, give furosemide and calculated hypertonic saline
e: This is TUR syndrome: dilutional hyponatraemia from absorbing non-sodium irrigant. Correct the sodium carefully, because correcting too fast risks central pontine myelinolysis.
s: Ch 146 Endoscopic and minimally invasive BPH therapy

q: The recommended irrigation height to limit fluid absorption during TURP is about:
e: Raising it 10 cm above this more than doubles fluid absorption. Symptoms usually start once sodium falls below 120 mmol/L.
s: Ch 146 Endoscopic and minimally invasive BPH therapy

q: Dark blood fills the irrigant during TURP but no bleeding point can be seen. Most likely source, and the usual remedy if diathermy fails:
o: Venous sinus bleeding; catheter with an over-inflated balloon on traction
e: Venous bleeding is darker and often stops when the bladder is full.
s: Ch 146 Endoscopic and minimally invasive BPH therapy

q: Resection in TURP conventionally begins with:
e: The verumontanum marks the distal limit, protecting the external sphincter.
s: Ch 146 Endoscopic and minimally invasive BPH therapy

q: Compared with monopolar TURP, bipolar TURP:
o: Practically eliminates TUR syndrome and reduces transfusion (relative risk about 0.53), with similar late complications
e: It uses saline. Bladder neck contracture and retreatment rates are not clearly different.
s: Ch 146 Endoscopic and minimally invasive BPH therapy

q: Transurethral incision of the prostate is best suited to:
o: Small glands (under about 30 mL); retrograde ejaculation in up to 37%, possibly less if unilateral
e: No tissue is removed and there is no TUR syndrome.
s: Ch 146 Endoscopic and minimally invasive BPH therapy

q: Which laser-safety rule is correct?
o: KTP energy is absorbed by irrigant
Only the surgeon needs eye protection
Eye protection is unnecessary with a video camera
Cover all windows and openings, post signs at every door, and protect the eyes of everyone including the patient
e: Holmium energy is absorbed by water, but KTP/LBO (green-light) energy is not. Both damage the eye in air.
s: Ch 146 Endoscopic and minimally invasive BPH therapy

q: Prostatic urethral lift implants are placed:
o: Anterolaterally, avoiding the neurovascular bundles and anterior veins
e: The book's criteria are a prostate under 80 g with no obstructing median lobe. It preserves erection and ejaculation, but long-term durability is less certain.
s: Ch 146 Endoscopic and minimally invasive BPH therapy

q: Men on anticoagulation having photoselective vaporisation (PVP) mainly have:
o: Longer hospital stay, more irrigation and longer catheterisation
e: Transfusion rates were not higher. PVP uses saline, so there is no TUR syndrome.
s: Ch 146 Endoscopic and minimally invasive BPH therapy

q: The suprapubic (transvesical) route is preferred over the retropubic route when there is:
o: A large intravesical median lobe, a symptomatic diverticulum or large bladder stones
e: For a large adenoma with a symptomatic diverticulum, do the prostatectomy and diverticulectomy together. Otherwise the diverticulum keeps emptying poorly and stays infected.
s: Ch 147 Simple prostatectomy

q: Which of these is the only ABSOLUTE indication for prostatectomy, according to the chapter?
o: Kidney damage caused by prostatic obstruction
e: The rest are relative indications. Contraindications include a small fibrous gland, significant cancer, and previous prostatectomy or pelvic surgery. The chapter advises against open simple prostatectomy below about 75 g (guidelines usually use more than 80 mL). HoLEP is now a size-independent alternative.
s: Ch 147 Simple prostatectomy
